title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Reproducible Ceiling/Null Result
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that measures the marginal effect of a deterministic verifier+repair pipeline (G→V→R) versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly on operator intent→configuration tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we selected K=200 tasks by a reproducible SHA‑256 sorting rule and evaluated a single shared generator output per task in both arms. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair step was never invoked. All execution, scoring, and validator traces are archived (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4...). We interpret this as a ceiling/null result specific to the tested model/task/validator regime, and we provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for designing failure‑rich verifier utility evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is operationally attractive but risky: mistaken applied changes can cause reachability regressions, service outages, and cascading operational faults. A common architectural pattern to mitigate these risks is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM proposes configuration commands, a deterministic verifier checks safety and workflow constraints, and a repair step attempts to correct violations before apply. While many prototypes and benchmarks advocate generate–validate–repair architectures, rigorous causal estimates of the verifier’s marginal effect under a reproducible, preregistered contract are scarce.

This manuscript reports a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived, paired experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that isolates the verifier+repair marginal effect by (i) fixing the generator output per task (shared_initial_generation) and (ii) comparing (baseline) accepting the candidate directly vs (guarded) running the candidate through the deterministic validator with at most one repair attempt. Key empirical facts (artifact anchors): K=200 paired tasks selected deterministically from an assembled public pool (task manifest SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...), requested model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed...), and raw run artifacts archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...).

Research question. Under a deterministic, reproducible sampling and execution contract, does a verifier+repair pipeline reduce regression‑causing changes compared with accepting an LLM suggestion directly? The preregistered primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in validator pass rates per task). Our contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired run with complete provenance and hash‑anchored artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded report of a ceiling/null outcome (no discordant pairs observed); (3) concrete, artifact‑grounded design recommendations for future failure‑rich evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and benchmarks motivate generate–validate–repair in NetOps and AIOps contexts and emphasize verifier‑integrated pipelines and solver grounding (examples: Cornetto — a network repair benchmark and generator→validator pipelines; TypoNet and work on formal verification and verifier evolution; broad surveys on LLMs-for-NetOps and agentic NetOps architectures).1–4 These works argue that operational reliability depends strongly on verifier and tooling design rather than model fluency alone. Our study differs by providing a preregistered paired causal estimate of verifier marginality under a tightly specified, replayable contract, with full execution and validator traces released for audit.

Selected artifact‑verified citations (archived during autonomous literature review) include Cornetto (arXiv:2604.22513) and recent position work advocating translation→solver architectures.5,6 (Complete cited_record_ids are listed in the manuscript package.)
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cand-002-gvr-loop before observing final outcomes (preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0bda22e...). The primary hypothesis H1: G→V→R reduces the regression‑causing change rate compared to LLM‑only suggestions (paired estimand). The preregistration froze task selection, validator, model scope (gpt-5-mini), maximum model calls, repair budget, and analysis plan (paired exact test + bootstrap CI).

Deterministic task sampling. Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and filtered to those covered by the preregistered deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Selection used a deterministic rule (compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, choose first K=200 unique tasks). The manifest and deterministic selection are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...). This deterministic selection prevents human selection bias and ensures replayability.

Shared_initial_generation and arm definitions. For each task a single generator call (shared_initial_generation) produced candidate_c; this same candidate_c was scored in both arms. Baseline: accept candidate_c and score post‑apply with the deterministic validator. Guarded: run candidate_c through the deterministic validator first; if the validator reports violations, the pipeline permits at most one automatic repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) to produce a repaired candidate, which the validator then rescores. Repair calls were constrained by the preregistration. The shared_initial design isolates the verifier’s marginal effect on fixed generator outputs but precludes generator adaptation to validator feedback.

Model, validator, and artifacts. Requested model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...). Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The deterministic validator parses generated commands to structured fields, enforces workflow policies (protected interfaces, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima), and yields a binary valid flag plus diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshot). All provider calls, model prompts/responses, scoring JSONs, and computed hashes were archived (execution/provider_calls/, execution/responses/, execution/scoring/; raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...). The master-run initial prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...).

Statistical analysis plan. The preregistered primary test is exact McNemar (two‑sided) on paired binary outcomes, supplemented by a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) to produce a 95% percentile CI for the paired difference. Power calculations were preregistered assuming baseline failure rate ≈ 0.20; note that such calculations depend on observed baseline prevalence and become inapplicable in degenerate ceiling regimes (see Results and Discussion). All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived (analysis/*; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 52a0858d...).
sections.results:
Execution and archival. Planned episodes: 400 (2 conditions × 200 tasks). Completed episodes: 400; completed model calls used: 200 (one shared initial generator call per task). No provider or infrastructure failures affected the scientific run. Key artifact anchors: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4..., execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 = 79c91155..., and execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...; representative scoring JSON examples reside under execution/scoring/ (e.g., task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 = 3055f874...).

Primary outcome (artifact‑grounded). Complete paired counts: complete_pairs = 200. Baseline validator passes = 200/200; guarded validator passes = 200/200. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The guarded repair pathway was never exercised: repair_applied = false for every guarded episode (see execution/scoring/*.json for per‑task validator traces).

Representative diagnostic excerpt. Each scoring JSON contains validator diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshot, and task difficulty metadata). For example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json records parsed_command_count=4 and validator.valid=true. A small representative subset (archived under representative_tasks) had the following difficulty composition: medium=1, hard=2, very_hard=3 (illustrative; full per‑task difficulty metadata for all K=200 tasks is retained in execution/scoring/*.json and is reproducibly aggregable by replaying those files; representative_tasks manifest and scoring JSONs are provided for audit). The run archive deliberately preserved per‑task difficulty fields rather than pre‑aggregating them during execution to maximize reproducibility of any user‑selected aggregation.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. The observed ceiling/null outcome (no discordant pairs) means that under the tested contract — deterministic selection of tasks covered by the validator, a single shared generator output per task, the requested model (gpt-5-mini), and the deterministic validator — all generated candidates already satisfied the verifier’s constraints. In this regime the verifier could not reduce regressions because none were observed in baseline. The paired exact and bootstrap inferences accurately describe the observed data: estimate 0.00, p=1.00, bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]. This is an artifact‑grounded ceiling/null result that does not imply that verifiers are unnecessary in failure‑rich production environments.

Why repairs were not invoked. Artifact‑anchored reasons explain the null outcome: (1) inclusion rule required validator coverage for tasks (task selection bias toward intents the validator supports); (2) the particular requested model produced well‑formed candidates that matched workflow constraints encoded in tasks (validator traces show normalized_configuration equal to candidates); (3) shared_initial_generation fixed generator outputs across arms and therefore prevented any generator adaptation that could have produced validator failures (repairs are invoked only on validator failure).

Design implications for future evaluations (artifact‑grounded guidance). To detect verifier/repair utility in confirmatory paired estimates we recommend: (a) sample or construct failure‑rich tasks (historical misconfigurations or adversarial boundary cases) so baseline failure prevalence is nonzero; (b) evaluate multiple generator strengths (add weaker models) to ensure variation in baseline success; (c) change the estimand if the goal is closed‑loop improvement — allow generator regeneration conditional on validator feedback and log all additional model calls; (d) publish per‑task validator coverage and difficulty aggregates together with paired counts — our archive preserves per‑task difficulty metadata and validator diagnostics to support such analyses (execution/scoring/*.json). The archived artifacts enable replay and re‑analysis under alternative sampling or interactive estimands.

Statistical note on degenerate CI and power. When no discordant pairs occur the empirical paired distribution is degenerate and the paired bootstrap reproduces identical resamples, yielding a point CI [0.00,0.00]; the exact McNemar two‑sided p becomes 1.00. This outcome makes the preregistered power calculation (which assumed baseline ≈ 0.20) inapplicable ex post. Reporting the degenerate CI and exact p is the correct descriptive inference for the observed regime and is fully reproducible from archived artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...).
sections.conclusion: Under the preregistered, deterministic, and fully archived contract (K=200 tasks selected by SHA‑256 sorting; shared_initial_generation; requested model gpt-5-mini), every generator candidate complied with the deterministic validator: baseline = 200/200; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair path was never invoked. This ceiling/null result is reproducible from the archived artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...). It does not generalize to failure‑rich or production distributions. Future confirmatory evaluations aiming to measure verifier utility should ensure nonzero baseline failure prevalence (via sampling or adversarial construction), vary generator strengths, and consider interactive generator–verifier estimands. All execution, scoring, and validator traces are released to support replay and extension by the community.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.

Synthetic deterministic task pool and the preregistered inclusion rule (validator coverage required) limit external validity to production intent distributions that contain emergent or historical misconfigurations.
Construct validity is tied to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; if the validator lacks coverage for real regression modes, the binary outcome conflates true safety with validator reach.

Design constraint: shared_initial_generation fixes the generator output for both arms and prevents generator adaptation; the experiment therefore measures verifier marginality on fixed candidates, not closed‑loop generator–verifier improvement.
Observed ceiling (baseline success = 100%) rendered the preregistered power calculation inapplicable; inference is descriptive and artifact‑grounded for the tested regime.
